theorem annihilator_iSup (ι : Sort w) (f : ι → Submodule R M) :
    annihilator (⨆ i, f i) = ⨅ i, annihilator (f i) :=
  le_antisymm (le_iInf fun _ => annihilator_mono <| le_iSup _ _) fun r H =>
    mem_annihilator.2 fun n hn ↦ iSup_induction f (C := (r • · = 0)) hn
      (fun i ↦ mem_annihilator.1 <| (mem_iInf _).mp H i) (smul_zero _)
      fun m₁ m₂ h₁ h₂ ↦ by simp_rw [smul_add, h₁, h₂, add_zero]

open Pointwise

variable {A : Type*} [CommRing A] {G : Type*} [Group G] {W : Type*} [AddCommMonoid W] [Module A W]
  {ρ : Representation A G W}
informal_statement: For any two subrepresentations ρ₁ and ρ₂, the toSubmodule of their intersection is equal to the intersection of their individual toSubmodules.
informal_proof: This equality holds by definition, as both sides represent the same concept of taking the toSubmodule of the intersection of ρ₁ and ρ₂.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
